_what: C-9 T9-0 (R-C9-71): 'lit world' mode, L toggles painted <-> lit. Painted is the default, so everything already play-tested is unchanged.
props_in_lit_mode: shaded as cards. They lose the highlights painted into them and read flat and dark next to a lit figure -- worst on the tree canopy, which in painted mode carries its own dappled light and in lit mode becomes a dark silhouette. This is the clearest argument in the capture for making them real 3D.

painted_prop_cards_are_NOT.bridge_post_card: 1.732 m tall vs the modelled post's 1.20 m -- 1.44x
painted_prop_cards_are_NOT.stump_a: 1.716 m -- a tree stump as tall as a man

scale.the_finding: the painting's props and the painting's FIGURE agree with each other at 1.25178; the blockout's geometry is at true scale and disagrees with both. Matt's 'he is too large' is the same disagreement seen from the other side: at 1.0 he agrees with the bridge he is standing on and no longer agrees with the stumps beside it.

terrain_ink: built and rendering, 14 meshes, same 1.1 output px as the figure -- the meshes are already in world metres so there is no per-mesh scale to undo. It reads heavier on a 40 m box face than on a man, because the line is a constant screen width and the silhouette it traces is 20x longer. Visible along the cliff edge in T9_bridge.jpg.
verdict: IT DEPENDS ENTIRELY ON WHICH WAY A SURFACE FACES. On open hillside that faces the key -- the tree path -- lit mode costs 16% of the mean luminance and crushes 0.03% of the frame: it reads as a slightly warmer, more saturated version of the same picture. On the bridge, where the cliff wall faces away from the key, near-black goes from 1.70% to 19.05% of the frame and 16.21% of the frame loses more than half its light. The cliff face is a 98 x 40 m greybox wall: its normal is a flat box face with no relation to the detailed cliff the painter shaded, so N.L and the painted shading disagree completely and the surface goes out.
what_L_switches: four things at once, because any one alone answers nothing: the terrain takes a SHADED projector and starts casting and receiving shadows; the sun stops being masked to the character and lights everything, with shadows on, in the same direction the painting's key implies; the props take a shaded card; and the character drops to TRUE SCALE 1.0.
